title: LBMA Precious Metals market volumes, June-August 2026, and their significance
author: StoneX
description: Early easing, consolidation then a n August recovery. Hormuz and bonds (naturally intertwined) the key driver; bond markets treat intervention with some disdain
content: AI Summary Summarize with Google AI Summarize in ChatGPT Explore with Perplexity Analyze with Claude Get Insights via Grok Key Takeaways Precious metals experienced three distinct phases during June-August 2026: early weakness, summer consolidation, and a strong recovery in August. Silver remained the strongest performer, gaining approximately 159% over the previous year. ETF holdings increased and speculative long positions expanded significantly during August, reflecting renewed investor confidence. Options volumes nearly doubled compared to the same period in 2025, highlighting increased hedging and speculative activity. The LBMA precious metals market between June and August 2026 was defined by a transition from correction to recovery. Early easing, consolidation then a n August recovery. Hormuz and bonds (naturally intertwined) the key driver; bond markets treat intervention with some disdain Rhona O’Connell, StoneX Financial Ltd; 4 th September May 2026 Any views expressed here are of the writer and do not reflect a house view from NASDAQ. Welcome to our monthly round-up of the LBMA OTC trading volumes in gold, silver, platinum and palladium, as recorded on a daily basis by the Association. These are split into spot, swap/forward, options and LoanLeaseDeposit (LLD) and give a flavour of the markets’ activity and how they were influenced by external forces and news items. Due to technical issues plus some holiday leave, this piece looks back at the June-August this year against June-August 2025 All references to COMEX or NYMEX positioning refer to Managed Money, not commercial positions. General introduction: Daily June-August average compared with daily average for the equivalent period in 2025. Source: LBMA Source: LBMA, StoneX Colour coding ranks the metals against each other in each sector June to August was a particularly eventful period for the precious complex, with the intersection of a hawkish new Fed, an interventionist Treasury, a re-escalating Gulf war, and a structurally weak dollar. Gold, silver, platinum and palladium, September 2025 to early September 2026 Source: Bloomberg, StoneX Silver still the outperformer at +159%; Platinum 125%, Gold 124% and palladium, 118% The three key drivers overall included the vicissitudes of the Gulf war, a dollar that was weak against the euro while strong against the yen – although it could be argued that the yen was independently weak - and a virtual tug-of-war developed between Fed Chair Kevin Warsh and US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessen, which is particularly relevant for gold. By the end of the period, the dollar-debasement argument, which had been fading, reasserted itself. After the rally in May, especially in silver, all four metals drifted lower through June and July as the summer doldrums set in and once again some major players were unwilling to take strategic positions. The dollar strengthened in June during the ceasefire in the Gulf but once escalation had resumed the currency entered a downward path that only paused for breath in late August. The metals did rally in late June as the Gulf ceasefire failed, with reciprocal strikes between the US and Iran raising new doubts over the return of shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. As we write in early September those doubts have still not been dispelled. In the background it was interesting to see the rising correlation between Brent and the US 10Y yield, but not that surprising since they are both rooted around the Gulf conflict and by definition gold forms part of this matrix also. Growing correlation between Brent and the US 10Y yield since the onset of hostilities Source: Bloomberg, StoneX January 2025 – early September2026 spot volumes, tonnes Gold Silver Source: for all charts above; LBMA, StoneX Platinum Palladium COMEX, NYMEX, positioning to 25 th August 2026 GOLD SILVER PLATINUM PALLADIUM Source: CFTC, StoneX Gold Gold sold off hard in June then spent July trading around $4,100 and occasionally dipping toward $4,000 in one interesting development, gold opened lower on July 13 and fell further despite the US–Iran airstrikes over that weekend, a telling sign that the hawkish-Fed/yield story was overriding the geopolitical safe-haven bid at that point. From a mid-July trough just below$4,000, the metal then staged its best stretch of the year, rallying: by 18% from its mid-July low to an intraday high of $4,696 on August 25 th , its highest since mid-May, before snapping a five-day winning streak late in the month after US inflation data came in above target, then steadying near $4,400–$4,600 into month-end. That mid-August week was gold's best since January, and gold-mining stocks had their hottest five-day run since 2008. Inverted gold and the real two-year yield Source: Bloomberg, StoneX It may seem counter-intuitive that gold prices were rising in the face of continuing increases in bond yields, but this is explained as follows. Yields were rising on inflation and fiscal fears rather than growth; a widening fiscal deficit, inflation persistently above 2% (for 65 months above target as Keviin Warsh noted in his Jackson Hole presentation at end-August), a weaker dollar, and an avalanche of corporate bond issuance to fund AI and data-centre build-outs — which is precisely an environment in which gold can flourish. Second, and probably more significantly, the Treasury Secretary’s efforts to suppress yields via FX intervention (something which almost invariably fails) were seen by the markets as an effort at fiscal dominance and financial repression: an admission that the debt load could no longer tolerate market-clearing rates. Sure enough, by early September 30-year yields were back over 5.2%. The US 5Y-30Y curve; long-term Source: Bloomberg, StoneX Adding to gold’s August rally were soft inflation numbers, but not soft enough for the Fed and Mr Warsh’s Jackson Hole comments were visibly more hawkish than the post-FOMC Press conferences held previously. Trading activity Turnover, M ounces Source: NASDAQ, LBMA As far as market turnover is concerned, the sell-off in early June was in the heaviest volume of the period, with over 30M ounces traded on each of three consecutive days. The rest of June was relatively busy but turnover in July was paltry. After some improvement in early August, the 5 th was particularly heavy as optimism grew over the possibility of Hormuz being reopened and with hedge funds getting on board gold rallied from $4,066 to $4,268, laying the foundations for consolidation in a new range, and latterly for the rally to almost $4,700 at month-end. That rally was in relatively thin conditions until the high-volume sell-off on the 28 th in the wake of Kevin Warsh’s comments. Gold from September 2025 Source: Bloomberg, StoneX Among the OTC derivative sectors, swaps/forwards were sluggish in June until towards month-end when, after falling below the 10-day moving average, forward activity picked up and helped to drive the price to the low for the period ($3,943 intraday). Activity increased in July and on more than one occasion seemed to be related to technical indicators, notably the moving averages. This was mirrored to an extent in the LLD segment, notably in early mid-July where heavy activity around $4,100 suggests that there was some supply-side hedging going through the market as prices failed at this level. As LLD volumes drifted off, the path higher became easier and indeed there was only one LLD trading day in August and that came on the 5th, quelling an initial attempt to clear $4,400. Volumes were high in mid-late July, with prices moving sideways, suggesting good two-way activity. After a busy day early in August, with a failed assault on $4,400, swaps/forwards tailed off. Finally the options market the volume over the period was almost double that of June-August 2025, with a daily average of almost 1.1M ounces. Even so, volumes were sluggish in June and July. The stand-out day, with 4.9M ounces going through was again 5 th August, along with high volumes in spot and swaps/forwards, suggesting that part of that swollen volume was hedging against options exposure. This was on that same day when the market rallied off the 20-day moving average at $4065 to $4,268; i.e. the 5 th when on hopes that Hormuz would reopen. Over the period the ETF gold holdings opened at 4,121t, briefly continued the decline that had started in mid-May, but then turned higher to close Augst at 4,181t, a net year-to-date gain of 156t. CFTC figures show outright Managed money longs rising from 402t to 497t on 25 th August, while outright shorts fluctuated from 54t to 64t the following week, fluctuated around 50t for much of the rest of the period before short covering into 23t in early Augst ; they closed the period higher again, at 47t. Gold and the S&P (log-scales) Source: Bloomberg, StoneX Silver As usual, silver was the highest-beta play on the same macro forces outlined above, and once again it moved violently. After a January record near $121–$122, it had already halved by early summer, opening June at $74 before a two-leg tumble to $56 on the 24 th , and entering a five-week period in a sideways trend between$55 and $63. This set the scene for the August recovery, with silver reaching an intraday high of &1 on the 28 th before, with gold, going into reverse post-Warsh. Gold and silver action, correlation Source: Bloomberg As well as the major factors that drove gold and by association, silver, the latter metal also has its industrial character to address, given that 70% of silver fabrication (ex-investment) is in industrial uses. The June-quarter hawkish Fed hold at 3.50–3.75% and a divided committee hit silver's industrial engine directly, and the gold-silver ratio widened from a May low near 55:1 to about 69:1 by mid-July — a classic sign of silver underperforming gold in a risk-off environment. The same soft-data/weak-dollar cocktail that lifted gold then drove the August rebound, amplified by silver's leverage. The August rally was accompanied, and to some extent driven by, the return of Managed Monay longs (after quite an exodus earlier in the year), rising from 2,822t in mid-July to 3,444t in late August, while shorts were slower to respond, having continued to expand to 1,368t in mid-August (from 941t in mid-July) then contracting to 1,143t in late August. Gold:silver ratio Source: Bloomberg, StoneX Although the US economy is relatively resilient and the onset of AI, vehicle electrification and solar cells will combine to take silver into an expanding pre-investment deficit, in the immediate term these forces are muffled to a degree with the current surplus of solar cells (and a minor threat from copper) while the ebbs and flows of vehicle electrification are a matter of record – although this is more relevant to the PGM than to silver; see below. Turnover Source: NASDAQ Spot volumes were down 39% over the period compared with June-August 2025. With the exception of 5 th August, much mentioned in our gold comments (Hormuz hopes), silver’s spot volume fluctuations were similar to those of gold with high volume in the June retreat (thus making the market less crowded) and then a sluggish period through to mid-July. As prices stabilised spot activity cautiously increased, although volumes in the rally to $70, which was reached on 21 st August, were patchy. On the 21 st , volumes were much livelier. As hedging activity developed (increased volumes in swaps/forwards and options also) and called a halt to the rally. After three successive efforts to clear $70, the market capitulated and the sharp fall to $66 on the 28 th was in heavy spot volume (but not in the derivatives). Derivatives activity was heavy in June in swaps and forwards, which will certainly have been instrumental in the price fall and would to some extent have been self-fulfilling. The LLD segment was 25% down on the 2025 equivalent and here, too , was busiest in the June fall. There was some cautious interest in mid-August when silver was flirting with $65, suggesting some hedging, especially as the price didn’t clear that level at that stage. Finally there was activity at month-end as silver was again on the retreat. Platinum and palladium Platinum was the "cleanest" fundamental story of the four, driven more by physical scarcity than by the dollar. The market is expected to be in deficit for the fourth consecutive year this year, despite expected falls in auto and jewellery demand, while supply is likely to be broadly steady. South Africa accounts for roughly 72% of refined production, and that concentration was the summer's active risk. National primary output fell from about 5.3 million ounces in 2006 to roughly 3.9 million in 2025 and while looking steady this year it is expected to decline again next year. On the demand side, the hydrogen fuel-cell demand, while coming from a very low base, adds a new industrial floor. Palladium trades heavily on autos (80% of demand comes from catalytic converters in gasoline and hybrid vehicles) so it is exposed to two secular headwinds; platinum substitution and the rise of battery-electric vehicles. The June price softness reflected slower automaker procurement, soft electronics demand, caution in the jewellery sector, plus almost non-existent investment, while supply was steady. The July bounce was seasonal restocking rather than scarcity. The one genuine supply-side tail risk remains geopolitical — Russia is the world's largest palladium producer (nickel by-product), followed by South Africa (platinum by-product) so any escalation of sanctions on Russian metal would be the scenario that could override the surplus narrative, much as it did in 2022. This is still up in the air. Turnover Source: NASDAQ Platinum spot turnover was 49% down on the equivalent period of 2025, while options and LLD were both down by ~20%. Swaps/forwards were the only sector in the black, up by 21%. Trading volumes were choppy, with a couple of heavy days trading in spot in the first week as prices came extended a slide from $1,980 ,although this was not mirrored in the OTC derivatives. The sharp fall from $1,906 to $1,772 was one of those days, and Spot volumes dwindled thereafter as prices slid to $1,535 on 1st July. At this point spot and forwards kicked in, in a classic surge in volume in a price reversal and suggesting industrial forward buying, sparking a period of price consolidation, during which the only point of interest was heavy forward activity on the approach to $1,700, which failed, implying continued industrial interest and quite possibly inventory management. Early August saw heavy volumes in spot forwards and options as prices surged from $1,629 to$1,751, stemming from a second day of oil price declines and a weaker dollar (Gulf again), taking all the metals higher and precipitating a change of range. After a period of consolidation the rally to a four-time failed test of $1,900 enjoyed good volumes in everything except options and the reversal saw strong spot activity, suggesting profit taking / stale bull liquidation. Platinum, palladium and the ratio, five-year view Source: Bloomberg, StoneX Palladium prices moved closely in line with platinum over the period, with the correlation between the two not dropping below 0.84, and reaching 0.90 on occasion. Spot trading patterns were not that similar, however, with the early June fall being more of a thin volume slide. There was some intermittent interest in late July in both spot and forwards as the market started to benefit from its prior period of price consolidation, and setting the scene for the sharp jump in early August that had affected all four metals. Forwards were busy in late July on the approach to $1,300, while there was little options activity until mid-August as prices completed a bear move from the failure at $1,400. That failure had itself been accompanied by heavy LLD volume, suggesting some hedging activity. Platinum, palladium and the spread, five-year view Source: Bloomberg, StoneX

title: Slicing the ETF Market 9 Different Ways
author: Phil Mackintosh
description: See how the U.S. ETF market breaks down by total assets, value traded, and product count — revealing where passive, active and levered ETFs lead.
content: AI Summary Summarize with Google AI Summarize in ChatGPT Explore with Perplexity Analyze with Claude Get Insights via Grok Key Takeaways Three New Lenses: ETF market share sliced by total assets, value traded, and product count — each telling a different story. U.S. Stocks Dominate Assets: Sizable international and fixed income exposures; commodities and crypto punch above their weight in trading. Not All Passive: Passive holds 87% of assets and 92% of liquidity, but active funds make up 49% of ETPs and ~47% of 2026 inflows. Levered ETFs Trade Hot: Just a sliver of assets, yet 13.4% of daily value traded and 44.5% of share volume — used as trading vehicles, not buy-and-hold. Exposure Over Size: Passive giants dominate the core, but crypto, active, and levered products lead at the edges. Earlier this summer, we included a chart in our intern’s guide to exchange-traded funds (ETFs) that showed how ETF liquidity can be broken down. It highlighted the diversity of exposures now available in the ETF wrapper, from stocks and bonds to passive and active, as well as different portfolio leverage. Chart 1: ETF liquidity can be measured in many ways Today, we break that data down into three more ways. Instead of looking at share volumes, we look at market share by total assets, value traded and by the number of ETFs in each category. Each tells a different story about what investors and traders like about ETFs. Looking at ETF exposure by asset class One of the great things about ETFs is that they let investors use stock markets to invest in far more than stocks. The chart below looks at asset allocation across the three new metrics. Chart 2: U.S. ETF exposures by asset class – North American exposure dominates The majority of assets in U.S. ETFs hold U.S. stocks. However, there are sizable exposures to international stocks and fixed income. Drilling into liquidity, we see relatively more trading in commodities (gold) and cryptocurrencies (teal). Interestingly, the number of products is more evenly spread across all categories, highlighting an incredible amount of choice across all categories. Specifically, there are a large number of alternatives ETFs, which includes the ETFs with options and target date funds. Not all ETFs are index products It’s a common myth that ETFs are all index funds. This data proves that’s not (entirely) true. Chart 3: Passive ETPs win on total assets, but active strategies trade 10% of daily volumes To be fair, passive management still dominates assets and liquidity, with 87% of assets and 92% of liquidity. Things change at the fund count level. Active funds are 49% of all ETPs by count. Interestingly, ETFGI reports that active ETFs account for nearly half (47%) of fund inflows in 2026, with $529.96 billion in year-to-date net inflows. Looking at ETF leverage ETFs and futures could both be called “derivatives” as they represent a ticker that gets you exposure to something else. Futures have always been levered, with expiry rolls, margin and potential margin calls all part of managing a futures position. The recent evolution of “Perps” has created similar leverage for investors. Some ETFs also provide leverage (although by rule, U.S. leverage has been capped at a much lower 2-times, typically). Chart 4: Unlevered ETFs dominate assets and issuance, and are the majority of trading Despite representing a fraction of assets, levered ETFs account for roughly 13.4% of daily value traded. Mathematically, that shows they are being used as trading vehicles and not held as long as other ETFs. Interestingly, levered ETFs account for a much higher 44.5% of daily share volume. That’s because many levered ETFs have low stock prices – making their share volumes higher for the same value traded. So, what does this tell us? For much of the ETF market, the giant passive index trackers do have outsized share. But at the edges, the divergences are sharp. Levered products, crypto ETFs and active strategies each punch well above their weight in certain categories. The question might not be how big the ETF market is — but which type of exposure you actually want to buy.

title: Biweekly Investment Insights: Markets swirl
author: Yanni Angelakos
description: The Federal Reserve raising rates by 25 basis points and signaling at least one more hike by the end of 2026 as inflation pressures persist. Treasury 10-year yields closing above 5% for the first time since mid-2007. Oil back over $100. Calls for AI deployment to be reined in. U.S. equities in the weakest seasonal period (per Bank of America, the average S&P 500 return during September-October is -0.56% since 1928). There is no shortage of cautious signals for equities and risk assets in the interim.
content: Yanni Angelakos, Head of Investment Insights, Nasdaq Capital Access Platforms Mike Cho, CFA, Senior Research Analyst, Nasdaq Capital Access Platforms Tony Kristic, Senior Research Analyst, Nasdaq Capital Access Platforms AI Summary Summarize with Google AI Summarize in ChatGPT Explore with Perplexity Analyze with Claude Get Insights via Grok Key Takeaways Equities recalibrate amidst higher Treasury yields August inflation dynamics cemented the Fed raising rates by 25 basis points on September 16 Higher Treasury yields & calls for an AI industry-wide slowdown have pressured equities Earnings growth continues to be the focal point for equity returns as multiple expansion is pressured The Federal Reserve raising rates by 25 basis points and signaling at least one more hike by the end of 2026 as inflation persists. Treasury 10-year yields closing above 5% for the first time since mid-2007. Oil back over $100. Calls for AI deployment to be reined in. U.S. equities in the weakest seasonal period (per Bank of America, the average S&P 500 return during September-October is -0.56% since 1928). There is no shortage of cautious signals for equities and risk assets in the interim. Drawdowns are frequent during the course of the year—broader U.S. equities have averaged more than three pullbacks of 5%+ a year since 1930 (per Bank of America)—but there has only been one in 2026 (March). Per our Biweekly Chart in Focus, Treasury 10-year yields sustaining above 4.50% have tended to pressure Nasdaq-100® forward valuations over the past three years. That is why we suspect that it is unlikely that future equity appreciation will be driven by multiple expansion—instead, it will be about earnings growth which has driven total equity returns over the past year. While the aforementioned headwinds are likely to keep markets under pressure in the near-term given ongoing derisking, equity returns have broadened amidst wider, supportive earnings trends which continues to expand the opportunity set for investors. Biweekly Charts in Focus: Sustained Treasury 10-year yields >4.50% have been a headwind for equity valuations the past 3 years Source: Bloomberg. As of September 14, 2026. Details Latest inflation data cements Fed’s 25 basis point hike The Fed raised rates as expected on September 16 th by 25 basis points to a range of 3.75% to 4.00%, while the median FOMC projection is forecasting one more rate increase by year’s end. Although the median FOMC projection is not calling for additional rate hikes next year, eight policymakers supported raising by an additional 25 basis points by the end of 2027. For historical context, while the beginning and end dates of official Fed cycles can be debated, per Bloomberg, there have only been two single-hike Fed cycles since 1970 (June 1975 and March 1997). Similar to the June 2026 meeting, 18 out of 19 officials provided rate projections for 2026 and 2027, with Fed Chair Warsh the lone abstainer from submitting forecasts (as in June)—in-line with his public pushback on forward guidance. With the Fed raising rates and its hawkish tilt, it has likely gained credibility with the bond markets as it demonstrates that it is following through on its willingness to attempt to tackle inflation—which could help to keep a lid on Treasury yields relative to it not acting. Elsewhere, major central banks are also on the move to combat inflationary pressures: the ECB raised rates by 25 basis points on September 10 th , as expected, citing persistent inflation above target and the markets are pricing in a full 25 basis point hike by the BoJ on September 18 th . Market pricing for a 25 basis point hike at the September 16th FOMC meeting was practically solidified following the latest August inflation reports (Figure 3), against the backdrop of a relatively resilient U.S. economy. First, PPI rose 0.4% MoM—the largest monthly gain since May—and 5.4% YoY, a beat versus the 5.3% expected and a sharp acceleration from July's 4.8%. The headline was driven almost entirely by a 4.2% surge in energy prices, with food prices contributing a modest 0.1% (per Bloomberg). Core PPI, stripping out food and energy, came in at 0.2% MoM—a miss versus the 0.3% consensus. However, markets largely looked past the soft core print: jumps in airfares and hospital services within the PPI details, combined with upward revisions to July's level, neutralized the headline beat and kept the hawkish read intact. Then, the CPI headline matched expectations at 0.4% MoM and 3.4% YoY, unchanged from July. Per Bloomberg, more than a third of the monthly gain came from a 3.9% rebound in gasoline prices, with food up a modest 0.1%. The surprise was in core CPI, which rose 0.3% MoM against a consensus of 0.2%. On a YoY basis, core CPI came in at 2.4%, the slowest since March 2021, but the monthly acceleration was what moved markets. Digging deeper into core CPI components, shelter was a key driver, rising 0.3%—its largest monthly gain in three months—reversing two months of subdued readings and owners' equivalent rent also picked up. Beyond shelter, wireless phone services jumped notably, also contributing to the core beat. Figure 2: Equities weaker on average following the start of prior Fed rate hiking cycles before recovering Source: Goldman Sachs The most closely watched sub-component of the CPI report as it’s the closest proxy to core PCE—the Fed’s actual inflation target—given the lower shelter weight, is supercore CPI (services ex-shelter). This gauge rose 0.51% MoM (per Bloomberg’s proxy)—the fastest pace since January. This measure, which the Fed tends to view as the most persistent and policy-sensitive component of inflation, saw core services exert a broader influence than energy on the month, reinforcing that price pressures are not confined to volatile categories. Treasury 10-year yields closing above the key threshold of 5% for the first time since July 2007 have been driven by the recent inflation reports and, relatedly, the ongoing resurgence in oil prices (Figure 4). WTI crude oil is back over $100 following the latest escalation in attacks in the Iran war and as Saudi Arabia halted its East-West pipeline which was struck by multiple attacks on September 10th. This pipeline has the capacity to carry about 7 million barrels a day to a key hub on the Red Sea (per Bloomberg) and functioned as an integral bypass of the Strait of Hormuz. Figure 3: August CPI & PPI reports maintained the sticky inflation narrative Source: Bloomberg. Figure 4: Moves in Treasury 10- and 30-year yields have been a byproduct of higher oil prices recently Source: Bloomberg. As of September 14, 2026. Valuation headwinds vs. earnings tailwinds Per Baird Strategas and Figure 5, higher inflation regimes since 1950 have tended to coincide with lower trailing U.S. equity valuations. When focusing on this relationship since 2008, equity multiples have tended to expand despite steps-up in inflation. However, this was greatly skewed during the 2021-2023 inflation spike as equity valuations initially expanded as earnings collapsed but prices recovered rapidly due to the historic fiscal and monetary stimulus during Covid-19. As rates and the inflation backdrop pressure equity valuations, it will likely come down to earnings growth to be the predominant driver. Per the refreshed Figure 6, it has been earnings growth which has driven all of U.S. equity total returns on a net basis over the past year, and not multiple expansion. In the interim, elevated valuations can face headwinds without the shelter of earnings season. Figure 5: S&P 500 average trailing P/Es by inflation tranche Source: Baird Strategas. As of June 30, 2026. Figure 6: Equal-weighted equities have rallied strongly vs. cap-weighted since Q4 2025 Source: FactSet. As of September 14, 2026. Notes: residual is allocated to multiple expansion Also likely feeding into the recent market psyche is the concern that increasing calls from AI research and deployment leaders to slow development, in addition to data center moratoriums, could weigh on earnings expectations across the AI ecosystem. The policies and regulations around AI deployment have yet to take hold as U.S. policymakers must weigh instituting AI guardrails against losing ground to China in the AI race. In the interim, this latest AI rhetoric has contributed to the ongoing churn in equity markets which remains top-of-mind for us. Figure 7 shows how AI-linked proxies (e.g., semiconductors, U.S. large cap growth, Nasdaq-100) have underperformed since the prior peak in the Nasdaq-100 on June 2 nd , while value and small cap groups have outperformed. YTD returns for the likes of semiconductors and the Nasdaq-100 remain solid as do the returns for international, U.S. large cap value, and equal-weighted U.S. stocks—speaking to the broader opportunity set. We’d be remiss, though, if we did not flag the recent weakness in U.S. small caps relative to the mega cap tech cohort since the recent lows in Treasury 10-year yields on August 25 th , which immediately preceded Fed Chair Warsh’s Jackson Hole more hawkish speech on August 28 th . Given the greater sensitivity to changes in rates on account of their relatively higher floating rate exposure as a percentage of total debt—around 5.5x higher, per Bloomberg—the Nasdaq U.S. Small Cap TM Index (NQUSS TM ) is -4.4% versus the Nasdaq-100 which is -0.9% since August 25 th (as of September 15 th ). Figure 7: Only U.S. large cap value, small cap & U.S. large cap equal-weighted equities are positive since June 2 nd Nasdaq-100 highs Source: Bloomberg. As of September 14, 2026. As we’ve discussed in prior reports, the broadening of U.S. equity returns is consistent with the broadening of corporate earnings trends. As another example, Figure 8 below per Bank of America Securities’ U.S. equity strategy team speaks to this trend. With more than 80% of S&P 500 stocks growing EPS YoY in Q2 2026, that puts it in the 94th percentile [ZC2.1]of historical readings shown in Figure 8. The strong earnings construct for megacap tech is a clear example of solid corporate fundamentals. A market concern which has grown louder, though, has come as hyperscalers have issued more debt to support their massive capex initiatives. Net new debt levels have certainly increased which has caused market angst. That said, per Figure 9 below, a sampling of seven AI hyperscalers shows that approximately two-thirds of total capex is being funded by operating cash—which speaks to the high profitability and strong cash flows of these companies. For more details, please see the recent report from our Index Insights team. Figure 8: Improving earnings breadth across S&P 500 companies Source: Bank of America Merrill Lynch Figure 9: Total capex (AI & non-AI) by funding source amongst AI builders Source: Exponential View, Nasdaq Index Insights. Notes: Analysis based on company filings (funding identity: cash = capex – leases – debt); 2026E based on current company guidance. As of 8/10/26. Of the ~$863B in total capex, ~$550B is estimated to be AI-related. Seven AI builders: Alphabet, Amazon, CoreWeave, Meta, Microsoft, Nebius, Oracle. title: Banking on You Featuring Timberland Bank
author: MarketInsite
description: Janice and Warwick Bryant turned a lifelong dream into reality with a loan from Nasdaq-listed Timberland Bank, building Kaukiki Farms, a 150-acre working farm and wildlife conservancy on Washington's Key Peninsula that now stands as a model of community and land stewardship.
content: AI Summary Summarize with Google AI Summarize in ChatGPT Explore with Perplexity Analyze with Claude Get Insights via Grok Key Takeaways Janice Bryant and her husband, Warwick Bryant, turned their dream of farm ownership into reality by purchasing and developing Kaukiki Farms with support from Timberland Bank. The 150-acre farm is built on sustainable practices, producing grass-fed livestock while preserving wildlife habitats and natural resources. A long-standing relationship with Timberland Bank has supported multiple family and business ventures, highlighting the value of personalized community banking. The Bryants have created a lasting legacy by protecting 114 acres of their property through the Great Peninsula Conservancy, ensuring long-term environmental stewardship. Kaukiki Farms demonstrates how responsible farming, community partnerships, and conservation can coexist for future generations Buying the (Dream) Farm: The Story of Kaukiki Farms Janice Bryant was a 4H girl from Iowa. Her husband, Warwick, grew up on a sheep and beef farm in New Zealand. Together, with a property loan from Timberland Bank, they found themselves preserving an idyllic corner of the Pacific Northwest. "We literally bought the farm," said Janice, co-owner of Kaukiki Farms with Warwick. Nestled on 150 acres on Washington's Key Peninsula, Kaukiki was a dream come true for the Bryants: the kind of place that could be mistaken for a film set, where grass-fed Angus cattle and sheep graze while the surrounding forests, streams, and wildlife habitat are carefully conserved. "We'd both grown up on farms and always wanted to have one," said Janice. In 2007, the opportunity "came to us kind of by happenstance." Through a former business, the Bryants had become familiar with, and captivated by, the Kaukiki property. They approached the owner to work out a deal. "We rented for six months, which applied against our balance, agreed on a price, and then we managed to somehow wiggle, niggle, find our ways and get a mortgage." "We said, wow, if we can make this work, what a great way to bring our boys up in an environment like the ones we had, one they could really appreciate. And so that's kind of how it all started. It was trying to replicate our childhoods for our children." A farm built on care The Bryants raise sheep and cattle primarily on grass and hay grown right on the farm. They manage their pastures carefully and take a deliberate approach to the health of both their animals and the land. Nearly two decades later, Kaukiki has become much more than a family farm. It's a community-renowned operation, a source of locally raised food, a wildlife refuge, and a model of land stewardship the Bryants hope will endure long after they're gone. A family banking relationship Shortly after Timberland Bank opened its Gig Harbor, Washington, office, Chief Residential Loan Manager Richard Pifer was introduced to the Bryants through their realtor. Over the years, the relationship has grown into one rooted in family and community, as Timberland assisted the Bryants and their sons with personal and business ventures alike, including their son's newest endeavor, Kiwi Fencing. "My dad gave me a bit of advice a long time ago: you should always know your banker," said Janice. "But you want a bank that is small enough that you really know the people who are there. Timberland has been just that." "When you walk in, they know you. You have a relationship. And so we started that relationship with Timberland, and it's been fabulous over the years." Janice recalls her time as School Board President of the private school both families attended, when the school fell on hard times. "We had to refinance a loan with really no capital. I was able to sit down with Richard at Timberland and say, 'Richard, is there any way we can do something?'" "And he found a way to make it work. It's been great. I wander in with a full stack of checks because I'm running between balancing hay and kids and everything else, and they're always there to make sure it all comes together." A legacy of conservancy Perhaps the most meaningful chapter of this story is the original loan Timberland provided to help the Bryants build their dream home, a property now part of the Great Peninsula Conservancy, with 114 acres of land permanently protected for the benefit of the community. “We actually have water rights, which is rare, and it allows us to irrigate,” said Janice. The quality of Kaukiki's grass is essential to the quality of their beef and lamb products. In fact, the property has a fresh spring fed stream that runs through the middle of the farm. "We have other friends that live in our canyon," said Janice, referring to the wildlife. "They're animals that live on the grass as well, but we love having a spot for them to go. We'll sit at the pond at night with a bottle of wine and watch the bear come out." One of the things the Bryants love most about Kaukiki Farms is how it extends a legacy of farming and conservation to an area that has developed rapidly over the years they've owned it.

title: What's New in Quantum Computing? Nasdaq Explores the Sector's Rise in Innovation and Investment
author: Nasdaq Newsroom
description: According to McKinsey research, quantum computing could generate multi-billion-dollar enterprise value over the next decade, with an economic impact that could reach approximately $2.7 trillion by 2035.
content: Quantum computing has emerged as a rapidly growing sector. There has been an increase in companies developing the technology entering the public markets in recent years, private investment is accelerating, and Nasdaq Global Indexes has added quantum computing to one of its leading innovation indexes. According to McKinsey research , quantum computing could generate multi-billion-dollar enterprise value over the next decade, with an economic impact that could reach approximately $2.7 trillion by 2035. Quantum computing companies generated just over $1 billion in revenue in 2025 alone. "Quantum technology helps organizations solve problems that are currently costly, difficult, or impractical using classical computers," said Ilaria Sangalli, Head of Index Insights for EMEA at Nasdaq, who authored the index team's research on the quantum sub-theme. Potential applications include molecular simulation for drug discovery, portfolio optimization in finance, supply chain management, and cybersecurity. As emerging technologies require capital to scale, the trend is currently playing out in public markets. Fifteen Nasdaq-listed U.S. companies specializing in AI and quantum computing hardware and software, have a combined market capitalization of about $3.78 trillion. Three-quarters of those companies have listed since 2020, including the recent listings of D-Wave Quantum, Quantinuum, and IQM Quantum Computers, with the largest wave arriving in 2021 and a new cohort emerging in the last two years. [1] The pattern resembles earlier cycles in AI, cloud computing, and cybersecurity, when investors began to treat each as a distinct category. In the recent enhancement of the Nasdaq Global Artificial Intelligence and Big Data™ Index (NYGBIG™), quantum computing became a dedicated sub-theme alongside areas like deep learning, cloud computing, and big data. Since its launch, the index has followed a forward-looking, patent-driven approach designed to identify companies at the forefront of technological innovation. The effectiveness of this approach has been reflected not only in the index's ability to identify innovative companies, but also in its long-term performance. Since its launch on November 12, 2018, NYGBIG has delivered a total return of approximately 384% (22.8% on an annualized basis). This pattern of outperformance has continued throughout the recent AI-driven investment cycle. Since July 2023, NYGBIG generated a total return of 139% (33% on an annualized basis), outperforming the Nasdaq-100®, broader U.S. equities, and several established AI benchmarks. [2] Of the 1,181 companies with patent activity related to NYGBIG's sub-themes, 247 held patents connected to quantum computing. "This suggests that quantum computing is evolving beyond a niche research field into a distinct technology ecosystem," Sangalli said. Her analysis also notes American leadership in the field: U.S. companies account for 58% of the quantum computing contribution score, a measure of each company's share of recently approved patents compared with other companies active in the same field. [3] The research also found that in addition to pure-play companies, the enhancement brought in traditional hardware companies with significant patent activity in the field, which placed them primarily in the quantum computing sub-theme. The quantum sub-theme's inclusion is closely tied to its convergence with AI. Quantum systems could accelerate optimization and simulation tasks running on classical computers, while AI is being applied to quantum algorithm development and error correction. "The two technologies may reinforce one another rather than develop independently," Sangalli said. Investment continues to grow. Quantum technology startups attracted $12.6 billion in venture and private funding in 2025, more than six times the 2024 level, with roughly 90% directed at quantum computing specifically. Governments are engaged, viewing the technology as critical for national security and cryptography; the U.S. government announced about $2 billion in quantum commitments in May 2026 and has taken minority stakes in leading companies. Yet the funding mix has flipped. Public money made up about one-third of total investment in 2024 and just 3% in 2025. Sangalli expects interest in quantum to build as more commercial use cases emerge, with investors gaining exposure through a mix of pure-play quantum companies and larger technology firms investing in the technology through R&D spending, including patent development. The boundaries of the category will likely blur, much as they have elsewhere. "Would you call Microsoft an AI company nowadays?" she said. "It's much more." Sources: [1] Source: Pitchbook and Factset [2] Nasdaq and Bloomberg [3] Nasdaq AI Team, Nasdaq, IFI Claims. title: Building Community Through The OPEN: A Conversation with Chad Dammert Smith
author: Hannah Goodfriend
description: In this interview, Chad Dammert Smith, Head of Index Marketing, Americas and The OPEN NYC Chapter Lead, reflects on how Employee Networks create connection, visibility, and belonging at Nasdaq. He shares how leading The OPEN has expanded his sense of community, strengthened his leadership skills, and helped foster meaningful opportunities for LGBTQ+ employees and allies to engage, collaborate, and feel supported in the workplace.
content: In this interview, Chad Dammert Smith, Head of Index Marketing, Americas and The OPEN NYC Chapter Lead, reflects on how Employee Networks create connection, visibility, and belonging at Nasdaq. He shares how leading The OPEN has expanded his sense of community, strengthened his leadership skills, and helped foster meaningful opportunities for LGBTQ+ employees and allies to engage, collaborate, and feel supported in the workplace. 1. What leadership position have you taken on in your Employee Network, and what do you do in this role? I serve as the NYC The OPEN Chapter Lead. When I joined Nasdaq in April 2025, one of the first things I wanted to do outside of my day job was get involved with The OPEN. As I looked for opportunities to participate, I realized there wasn't active chapter leadership in the New York office, which felt like an opportunity to help build something meaningful. Employee Resource Groups have been an important part of my career since 2015, and I founded an ERG program at a previous company. Taking on this role felt like a natural extension of that experience. My goal has been to increase visibility, create opportunities for connection, and help foster a strong sense of community for LGBTQ+ employees and allies across the NYC office. 2. In your own words, what is the mission of your Employee Network? The OPEN exists to support, celebrate, and elevate the LGBTQ+ community and its allies at Nasdaq. We create opportunities for connection, education, advocacy, and visibility while fostering a workplace where people feel comfortable bringing their authentic selves to work. Through employee engagement and partnerships both inside and outside Nasdaq, we strive to build a stronger sense of belonging for everyone. 3. How has being an Employee Network Leader contributed to your professional development at Nasdaq? Leading The OPEN has expanded my perspective of Nasdaq far beyond my day-to-day role. It has connected me with colleagues across businesses, functions, and leadership levels, including executives I may not have otherwise interacted with. The experience has given me a deeper understanding of how Nasdaq operates as a company and reinforced the value of building relationships across the organization. I've learned that some of the most valuable insights come from conversations with people whose experiences and perspectives differ from my own. 4. What skills have you gained or improved since taking on an Employee Network leadership role? Although I had prior leadership experience before joining Nasdaq, leading OPEN while still relatively new to the company accelerated my learning in unexpected ways. It helped me better understand how Nasdaq works, how decisions are made, and how different parts of the business connect with one another. The experience has strengthened my ability to navigate the organization, build partnerships, and turn ideas into action. Having a broader understanding of the business helps me think more strategically about what's possible for OPEN and how we can create meaningful experiences for our members. 5. How has being in an Employee Network leadership role contributed to your sense of community at Nasdaq? The impact has been tremendous. Before taking on this role, most of my relationships were connected to my work within the Index business. Since becoming involved with OPEN, I've built meaningful connections with colleagues from across the company and around the world. Today, I recognize and engage with people from departments I may never have interacted with otherwise. Those relationships have made Nasdaq feel like a much smaller, more connected place, and they've strengthened my sense of belonging within the organization. 6. What does “integrity” mean to you as an Employee Network Leader? To me, integrity means creating an environment built on trust, respect, and accountability. As an Employee Network leader, I have a responsibility not only to represent the interests of our members, but also to ensure our work aligns with Nasdaq's values and standards. Integrity means following through on commitments, creating inclusive experiences, and making decisions that serve both the community and the broader organization. It's about ensuring OPEN remains a place where people feel welcomed, supported, and proud to participate. 7. What have you learned about leading a team or managing others in your role as an Employee Network Leader? One lesson that has remained consistent throughout my leadership journey is that people are most engaged when they feel ownership over what they're helping to create. Rather than directing every outcome, I try to create opportunities for collaboration and shared decision making. When people have a voice in shaping the direction of a team or initiative, they're more invested in its success. It also creates opportunities to learn from one another. Some of the best ideas come from perspectives that are different from my own, and I believe leadership works best when it's a partnership rather than a one-way conversation. 8. How have Employee Networks enabled you to honor your culture, heritage or background at work? As a gay man of mixed race, I've always experienced identity through multiple lenses. Employee Networks have given me an opportunity to celebrate those different parts of who I am while helping others do the same. Leading OPEN has also allowed me to build connections with other Employee Networks, creating opportunities to support one another and amplify our collective impact. The result is a stronger sense of visibility, representation, and belonging for employees across many different backgrounds and experiences. 9. What has been the most rewarding moment as an Employee Network leader? There have been many rewarding moments, from our quarterly socials to our Pride Month programming. But if I had to choose one, it would be seeing the growth and engagement of The OPEN NYC Pride Committee. Watching employees volunteer their time, contribute ideas, and help bring our programs to life has been incredibly rewarding. None of our accomplishments would have been possible without their passion and commitment. Seeing a community come together and rally around a shared purpose has been the most meaningful part of this experience. 10. How do Employee Networks contribute to in-office culture at Nasdaq? Employee Networks play a critical role in creating a vibrant and connected workplace culture. They provide opportunities for employees to build relationships outside of their immediate teams, learn from one another, and engage with experiences they may not encounter in their day-to-day roles. For many employees, Employee Networks become a gateway to broader connections across the company. They help transform a workplace into a community and create opportunities that might not otherwise exist. 11. What have you learned about your own or other cultures or communities as an Employee Network leader? I've learned that everyone has a story, and that our shared identities are often just the starting point. While common experiences can bring people together, it's our individual perspectives, backgrounds, and journeys that make communities truly meaningful. Leading The OPEN has reinforced the importance of listening and being open to learning from others. The more we understand each other's experiences, the more empathy, connection, and belonging we create within our workplace.

title: Chartstopper: September 18, 2026
author: Michael Normyle
description: For markets, the big themes this week were the Federal Reserve rate decision, developments in the Iran conflict, and AI model development.
content: AI Summary Summarize with Google AI Summarize in ChatGPT Explore with Perplexity Analyze with Claude Get Insights via Grok Key Takeaways Fed hikes 25bp, signals one more this year Oil holds above $100 amid Iran conflict developments AI safety debate sparks brief chip stock selloff 10-year yields near 2007 highs, Nasdaq-100® is up 1% This Week For markets, the big themes this week were the Federal Reserve rate decision, developments in the Iran conflict, and artificial intelligence (AI) model development. The Fed hiked 25 basis points and sees one more hike this year . The hike to 3.75%-4.00% was widely expected, and the Fed said the move supports “a timelier return” to the Fed’s 2% inflation target, given that “inflation remains elevated” while the economy is growing “at a solid pace.” From here, the median estimate calls for another hike this year, before leaving rates unchanged at 4.00%-4.25% all of next year. Markets, however, see another three hikes before rates stabilize in the second half of 2027 in the 4.50%-4.75% range. Oil prices hover above $100 per barrel as a Saudi pipeline is set to reopen at half capacity within days and China asks Iran to help “rein in” the Houthis. After closing its East-West pipeline last Friday following attacks, Saudi Arabia expects to reopen it at half capacity within days and at full capacity after six weeks. This pipeline helps bypass the Strait of Hormuz via getting oil to the Red Sea, but this route faces its own issues as Houthis have increasingly taken control of the southern exit from the Red Sea. This week, however, it was reported that China asked Iran to help “rein in” the Houthis , which could help ease oil prices, if successful. Debate over potentially slowing frontier AI model development to mitigate potential safety risks drove a temporary selloff in chips stocks , though they’ve since recovered. For the week, 10-year Treasury yields are up a few basis points to 5% – around their highs since 2007 – while the Nasdaq-100® is up 1%. title: NH - Creating New Horizons
author: MarketInsite
description: Serving the Korean local investors for more than half a century, NH Investments & Securities (“NHIS”), part of the country’s influential financial player Nonghyup Financial Group, has always been a pioneer in the local brokerage industry.
content: AI Summary Summarize with Google AI Summarize in ChatGPT Explore with Perplexity Analyze with Claude Get Insights via Grok Key Takeaways Client-first approach drives NHIS’ investment solutions and services. ESG and sustainability remain key strategic priorities. AI and digital innovation enhance research, security and client experience. Nasdaq collaboration gives Korean investors deeper access to U.S. markets. Investor education supports the next generation of investors. Serving the Korean local investors for more than half a century, NH Investments & Securities (“NHIS”), part of the country’s influential financial player Nonghyup Financial Group, has always been a pioneer in the local brokerage industry. With its continuous effort in establishing partnership with overseas key players, NHIS manages to identify global investment opportunities and market intel to its investors. Combined with its local experience and expertise, NHIS has successfully become a local broker that is able to provide local market access to global opportunities, innovative investment solutions and world-class client services. Latest Important Milestones Client Centric The core value of NHIS is client centric. This leading broker always ensure its clients are at the center of its business philosophy, operations and product ideas. The following key initiatives showcase how NHIS create new horizons by identifying new opportunities for its clients. “The way we operate our business and the resources allocation always center around the value enhancement we bring to our clients,” said Yoon Byungun, CEO of NH Investment & Securities. ESG Investment – NHIS is dedicated to sustainable investment. It strives to prioritize investments that meet the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals. The broker is also a leading company in the ESG bond market and contributes to the facilitation of ESG bond issuance and secondary markets. The broker adopts green management strategies to ensure carbon neutrality and aligns interest of management, stakeholders and the local community. Digital Transformation – With huge investment in technology, NHIS transformed its Wealth Management client platform with world-class digital infrastructure that makes timely delivery of market news and access to investment solutions seamlessly. It also developed an AI-based model that prevents unauthorized use of accounts which helps providing additional security to its clients. Investor Education – NHIS works closely with local universities and industry associations to ensure investor education is in place. Previous themes included blockchain, investment service for millennials investors and stock picks. In 2023, NHIS hosted its 4 th Big Data Contest with the objective of educating college and graduate students how to analyze financial data and how to collect the right market news for the right clients. Given the local investors’ appetite in the U.S. market, NHIS worked with Nasdaq who provided U.S. market data and RSS feeds for the participants of the contest – which made the 2023 contest unique as it was the first time during a contest of this nature when U.S. real time market data was offered. Winner of the contest was invited by NHIS to view Nasdaq’s Opening Bell Ceremony at the exchange’s headquarters MarketSite which is an iconic spot in New York. The special award is second-to-none in all the trading contests in Korea. It did not only create a special bond between NHIS and the next generation of investor community, it also educated investors the importance of diversification and how to tap U.S. investment opportunities. With investor interest at heart and is dedicated to investor education – the value shared by NHIS and Nasdaq – the contest was well received by the local community. U.S. Investing With a market cap of over USD50 trillion, the U.S. market is the largest and the most liquid in the world. It allows investors to own shares of the largest companies that have trait of robust growth and accelerated earnings. Diversifying investment with U.S. equities can help mitigate risk of concentrated portfolio of local stocks. Afterall, the U.S. markets include U.S. government bonds, corporate bonds, options, ETFs and even ADRs that provide access to non-U.S. companies. The market is transparent and is regulated by the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission which promotes market efficiency, integrity and investor protection. Why NHIS for U.S. Investing U.S. equities market is vibrant and competitive. Markets compete for listings, for order flow and to power the international trading communities’ tools, algorithms, and displays. To provide transparency and access to the U.S. markets, NHIS collaborates with Nasdaq to provide Nasdaq’s golden source for U.S. equity data. Nasdaq’s real-time market data products are provided to millions of users, powering price discovery and investment decisions across the globe. “Our active retail investors who trade U.S. equities market are demanding access to more granular information. Nasdaq TotalView offers the most complete information investors need to bring their active trading to the next level,” comment Yoon on the importance of Nasdaq TotalView, a premium data feed that displays full order book depth on Nasdaq, including every single quote and order at every price level in Nasdaq-, NYSE- and regional-listed securities trading on Nasdaq. Looking Ahead Ongoing investment is made in AI and big data analysis technology. NHIS explores AI and big data analysis model which can work seamlessly with its well-established traditional statistical methodology to ensure quality research is delivered. NHIS implements various ESG management activities to establish a sustainable management system. In order to implement the goal of being carbon neutral, the firm led the way in sustainable carbon neutral growth by declaring coal phase-out finance on February 2021 and have since then accelerated new Carbon Finance projects, such as creating an emissions trading market. As a digital innovator in the industry, NHIS ensures sufficient investment and effort are made in talent and technology development. There are a few collaboration projects with research institutes such as KAIST, a local science and technology university, and Seoul National University which look into tech that can drive digital finance innovation initiatives.

title: Green Team Spotlight: Growing a Greener Nasdaq with Alexandra Kornberger
author: Hannah Goodfriend
description: As Global Co-Lead of the Green Team Employee Network, Alexandra Kornberger is helping bring sustainability to life across Nasdaq through education, volunteerism, awareness campaigns and in-office experiences that spark connection. In this interview, she shares how leading the Green Team has strengthened her professional growth, deepened her sense of community and empowered employees to make a positive environmental impact at work and beyond.
content: As Global Co-Lead of the Green Team Employee Network, Alexandra Kornberger is helping bring sustainability to life across Nasdaq through education, volunteerism, awareness campaigns and in-office experiences that spark connection. In this interview, she shares how leading the Green Team has strengthened her professional growth, deepened her sense of community and empowered employees to make a positive environmental impact at work and beyond. 1. What leadership position have you taken on in your Employee Network, and what do you do in this role? As a Global Co-Lead for the Green Team Employee Network, I help drive employee engagement around sustainability across Nasdaq through educational programming, volunteer opportunities, awareness campaigns, and events. 2. In your own words, what is the mission of your Employee Network? The mission of the Green Team is to empower Nasdaq employees to create a positive impact by adopting environmentally conscious practices and promoting sustainability both at work and in their local communities. 3. How has being an Employee Network Leader contributed to your professional development at Nasdaq? Serving as a Global Co-Lead of the Green Team has contributed to my professional development by providing me with the opportunity to collaborate with colleagues and senior leaders across the business and build cross-functional relationships. When you take on an employee network leadership role, you learn firsthand what it means to be a culture carrier at Nasdaq. 4. What skills have you gained or improved since taking on an Employee Network leadership role? Since taking on the Employee Network leadership role, I have strengthened my leadership, project management, and stakeholder engagement skills. Leading initiatives, such as the planning committee for our Inaugural Sustainability Fair at our New York office, strengthened my ability to execute large-scale initiatives and drive successful outcomes. 5. How has being in an Employee Network leadership role contributed to your sense of community at Nasdaq? This role has deepened my sense of community at Nasdaq by allowing me to collaborate with colleagues across regions that I might not have interacted with in my day job. These connections have exposed me to different perspectives, expanded my understanding of the business, and provided me with valuable institutional knowledge, fostering a stronger sense of belonging to the Nasdaq community. 6. What does “integrity” mean to you as an Employee Network Leader? As an Employee Network Leader, integrity means leading with authenticity. Network leaders have the opportunity to shape the culture at Nasdaq, and I have strived to create an environment on the Green Team that mirrors Nasdaq’s values and supports collaboration and innovation. 7. What have you learned about leading a team or managing others in your role as an Employee Network Leader? As an Employee Network Leader, I’ve gained many learnings about leading a team and managing others, such as the importance of empowering team members and making them feel heard and valued. It is important to bring calmness, confidence, and stability to the team, especially during times of uncertainty or change. 8. What has been the most rewarding moment as an Employee Network leader? One of the most rewarding aspects of this role has been seeing Green Team members across regions bring their innovative ideas to life and successfully deliver meaningful initiatives within their local chapters, such as the New‑to‑You Gift Swap in our Vilnius office, which was a sustainability initiative designed to reduce waste and extend the life of everyday items. Since I am based out of the New York office, I was proud to successfully host our Inaugural Sustainability Fair, in which we welcomed sustainability-focused guest exhibitors, which included Nasdaq-listed companies, Lucid Motors, Oatly, and Beyond Meat, and nonprofit organizations such as the New York Botanical Garden (NYBG). One of the highlights of the Fair was NYBG's orchid care workshop, where an orchid specialist shared expert tips and guidance. 9. How do Employee Networks contribute to in-office culture at Nasdaq? Employee Networks contribute to in-office culture at Nasdaq by creating a sense of community and belonging for employees and providing engaging experiences. These in-person events often spark new connections and insightful conversations. In my experience, whether it’s bonding over bonsai trees or business (the Green Team hosted a bonsai tree workshop at our New York office last year), I have found that in-office events can be catalysts for connection and innovation.

title: Treasury hits Russia's VTB Bank with new sanctions over Iran ties
description: The new Russian bank sanctions follow a small handful of other actions that the Trump administration has taken since vowing to inflict "economic D-Day" on Iran.
content: A photo shows an exterior view of a branch of Russia's VTB Bank, on May 23, 2023 in Tehran, Iran. Fatemeh Bahrami | Anadolu Agency | Getty Images The Treasury Department on Monday announced new sanctions on Russia's state-controlled VTB Bank as part of its effort to economically isolate Iran by targeting its business partners and other financial "enablers." The action, which followed Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent's promise that a "large bank" would be sanctioned on Monday, was the latest penalty to be doled out as part of "Operation Economic Outcast," the Trump administration's non-military warfare strategy against Iran. The new sanctions against VTB Bank Public Joint Stock Company, Russia's second-largest bank, stemmed from allegations that it helped Tehran evade sanctions in part by "establishing correspondent relationships with sanctioned Iranian banks." The new financial action, which Treasury expects to block at least tens of millions of dollars, makes VTB "among the most comprehensively sanctioned financial institutions in the world," Treasury said in a press release . That's because the bank was already sanctioned by the U.S. in 2022 and early 2025 under the Biden administration. But curbing the bank may indirectly lead to economic limits on China, which is the top buyer of Iran's oil. Some observers were quick to raise questions about how much of an impact the new sanctions would have. "We're still digesting it a little bit," Tobin Marcus, head of U.S. policy and politics at Wolfe Research, told CNBC following Treasury's announcement. While VTB is a large bank in Russia, it has already been significantly sanctioned, Marcus noted. "The devil does tend to be in the details," he said. "Under Operation Economic Outcast, Treasury will continue to target and disrupt those who provide material, technological, or financial support that allows the Iranian regime to sustain its terrorist enterprise," Bessent said in a statement. "Treasury will not tolerate any support to the regime and will continue to identify, expose, and isolate Iran's enablers." Monday's action follows a small handful of other sanctions the Trump administration has imposed since last month, when it vowed to unleash "economic D-Day" on Iran and hobble its regime through global economic pressure. Read more CNBC politics and policy coverage Analysis: Hot inflation data sets up a Fed rate hike. What happens if Warsh wavers Hassett kept up to $5 million Coinbase stake as Trump reshaped crypto policy Trump's energy holdings have surged as the Iran war moved oil markets The new sanctions also drew questions about a potential indirect impact on China, Iran's top trading partner and oil buyer. VTB is reportedly the only Russian bank with a branch in China. "This is a China play," Miad Maleki, a senior fellow at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies and former U.S. Treasury sanctions official, said in an X post. "What changes today: every Chinese bank touching VTB Shanghai now carries Iran-program secondary-sanctions exposure, inside an operation where Treasury is naming a bank a week," Maleki wrote. "Beijing has shielded its big banks from the Russia fight. Shielding them from the Iran fight is a different calculation," he wrote, noting Chinese President Xi Jinping is expected to meet with President Donald Trump later this month. title: Counting the votes: Warsh faces a tough battle as the Fed girds for expected interest rate hike
description: Traders were pricing in a better than 92% probability of a rate increase, as well as a more than 75% chance for another one in December.
content: Kevin Warsh, chairman of the US Federal Reserve, during a news conference following a Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting in Washington, DC, US, on Wednesday, June 17, 2026. Al Drago | Bloomberg | Getty Images Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh faces a tricky head count this week when he and his fellow policymakers decide on both the immediate and future path of interest rates. While markets have honed in on a near-certain quarter percentage point hike in Wednesday's vote, it's not at all clear how broad will be the margin among the 12 Federal Open Market Committee voters. Moreover, Warsh will have to decide how to message the move: Will this be the rare one-and-done on hikes, will there be more to come or will the chair maintain his cryptic posture in not trying to guide markets one way or the other? "With the market priced this way, it would be shocking if he came in and did nothing," Bill Dudley, the former New York Fed president, said in a CNBC interview. "It would really damage his credibility because it would basically be all talk, no action." Indeed, as of Monday afternoon, futures traders were pricing in a better than 92% probability of a rate increase this week, as well as a more than 75% chance that the FOMC would follow up in December with another move, according to the CME Group's FedWatch gauge. Fed funds, the benchmark overnight borrowing rate, currently stand at 3.50% to 3.75%. The greater probabilities follow another run-up in fuel prices and inflation data last wee k that showed prices continued to climb in August. Both trends followed Warsh's comments a few weeks ago that the Fed would be forced into action unless there are more concrete signs that inflation is easing back to the central bank's 2% target. However, there are substantial complications. Wait or act? For one thing, the Fed historically has looked through the type of trends that are fueling inflation now. Economists generally agree that much of this year's increase has come from tariffs and an energy supply shock from the Iran war, both of which have uncertain impacts on the long-range trajectory of inflation. "We do not see a strong economic case for raising the funds rate," Goldman Sachs economist David Mericle said in a client note. "We think that all of the overshoot of 2% can be attributed to one-time factors whose impact is likely to fade." Nevertheless, Goldman changed its call from no change at this week's meeting to a hike, primarily because the firm's economists think the market expectations will force the Fed to move. Whether that also will be the case on an FOMC that voted 9-3 in favor of a hold at the July meeting is another matter. The three dissenters — regional presidents Lorie Logan of Dallas, Beth Hammack of Cleveland and Neel Kashkari of Minneapolis — all supported a quarter-point hike two months ago, when the Fed last met. Assuming their positions haven't changed, and there's been nothing in their public comments to suggest they have, that would mean four other members would have to switch their votes from hold to hike. Arguably the most-watched voter is Governor Christopher Waller. In public remarks delivered Sept. 3, Waller voiced suppor t for another hold at this meeting, albeit with the usual caveats about watching data to confirm that disinflation trends are continuing. Mostly, he merely urged patience rather than a rush to hike. "What's the cost of waiting one meeting? Hiking 25 basis points, one meeting right now, is not going to bring the [consumer price index] down to 2%," he said. The CPI for August actually showed headline inflation running at a 3.4% rate, though the core rate, which excludes food and soaring energy costs, was a more benign 2.4%, down 0.1 percentage point from July. Waller wasn't alone in advocating patience — New York Fed President John Williams told CNBC less than two weeks ago that a "wait-and-see" approach seems to make sense. Earlier in the summer, Williams, whose perch atop the New York Fed is traditionally considered part of the influential "troika" of influence at the central bank, said he thinks inflation has peaked . Also in recent remarks, Governor Michael Barr expressed concern about temporary inflation taking deeper hold and said he would be open to a hike, not set on one. The FOMC breakdown So who would join the three July dissenters? Warsh is largely expected to be part of the hiking group, considering his remarks in Jackson Hole, Wyoming last month. Governor Lisa Cook said in early August that she's "prepared to act" to take on inflation. Conversely, Philadelphia Fed President Anna Paulson and Chicago's Austan Goolsbee also have counseled a more patient approach. That would leave Governors Philip Jefferson, who is the vice chair; Jerome Powell , the former chair, who has kept a decidedly low profile since stepping down from the top spot, and Michelle Bowman, who spoke little on monetary policy over the summer and whose last related remarks were in May, when she also expressed concern about hiking unnecessarily. Then there's a larger wildcard: Should Warsh press the case for a hike, would those on the fence simply cross over to his side in the interest of presenting a united front? The vote margin not only will reveal the extent of the intellectual divide on the committee between those who think inflation is temporary and those who believe price pressures are becoming entrenched. It also will provide important signals about how effectively Warsh's leadership is reverberating inside the Fed. "It should be noted that, if the Fed does indeed raise rates this week, it may not look, in retrospect, like a close call," David Kelly, chief global strategist at JPMorgan Asset Management, said in his weekly market note. "If a majority within the committee coalesces around a decision to hike, the other members may well join them to portray a more united front to the public and the President." In such a case, Kelly said the final vote could see two, one or no dissents. From there, markets will look at the Fed's "dot plot" update. The grid spells out, anonymously, the rate expectations for the full 19 participants at the meeting, though Warsh withheld his dot for the June update. Investors will look for how much conviction there will be for two hikes this year, as well as the outlook for 2027. This will also feature the first look at 2029. The Fed almost never hikes or cuts just once but rather moves in cycles, as policymakers view incremental one-off moves as ineffective. A 10-8 split in favor of one hike — assuming Warsh's disdain for forward guidance and nonparticipation in the update — would indicate that "some participants might be ambivalent about the first hike and some might want to avoid pushing market expectations any higher," Mericle wrote. "But we see a risk of a majority for two hikes if more participants than we expect see a hike this week as a normal response to higher oil prices and AI demand and the start of a series of rate hikes," he added. In the case of a close divide on the committee, attention then will turn to Warsh's news conference Wednesday afternoon, and how the chair conveys FOMC sentiment. Dudley, the former New York Fed chief, said "the Fed needs to explain how they're thinking about the economy." "Now [Warsh has] just got to follow that up with action," Dudley said. "If he does that, I think he's basically fixed the problem that he created in his first two press conferences."
